title: Selecting Metals & Heat Treatment
description: How function, cost, aesthetics and environment guide metal selection; stock forms; heat treatment processes.
content_html:
Factors Influencing Metal Selection

Choosing the right metal for a product is rarely straightforward. Designers must balance a range of sometimes competing factors to arrive at the most appropriate choice. No single property determines the decision — a metal that is mechanically perfect may be too expensive, too heavy or impossible to source in the required stock form.

The principal factors are:

  • Function — the mechanical demands placed on the product. A bridge cable must have very high tensile strength; a cooking pot must conduct heat efficiently and resist corrosion from food acids. The function defines which properties are non-negotiable.
  • Cost — raw material cost, ease of machining and finishing all affect the final product cost. Mild steel is cheap and easy to process; titanium offers outstanding strength-to-weight ratio but costs approximately 50 times more per kilogram.
  • Aesthetics — appearance matters for consumer products. Copper has a warm, distinctive colour and develops a patina; polished stainless steel projects a modern, hygienic image. Anodised aluminium can be given vivid colours for consumer electronics and sporting equipment.
  • Availability — even the ideal metal is useless if it cannot be sourced in the required quantity, lead time or stock form. Exotic alloys may only be available from specialist suppliers with long lead times, disrupting production schedules.
  • Environment — the operating environment determines corrosion resistance requirements. A boat hull operates in salt water; a storage rack in a dry warehouse faces very different corrosion risks. Materials used in food contact must comply with food-safety regulations.
Key Fact

A complete metal-selection answer must address at least two factors: the key functional property (e.g. tensile strength, corrosion resistance) and one additional factor (cost, availability, aesthetics or environment). Answers that only cite one property will not reach the higher mark bands at Eduqas.

Stock Forms

Metals are supplied commercially in a range of stock forms. Selecting the appropriate stock form reduces the amount of material that must be removed and can simplify manufacturing. Common metal stock forms include:

  • Sheet and plate — flat, rolled metal. Sheet is typically under 3 mm thick; plate is 3 mm and above. Used for car body panels (sheet steel), structural decking (plate steel) and roofing (copper sheet).
  • Bar and rod — solid sections with circular, square, hexagonal or rectangular cross-sections. Hexagonal bar is used for nuts and bolt blanks; round bar is turned on a lathe to produce shafts and spindles.
  • Tube — hollow cylindrical or square section. Used in bicycle frames (lightweight tubing), handrails and scaffolding. The hollow section gives a high strength-to-weight ratio.
  • Angle section — L-shaped cross-section, used in shelving frameworks, brackets and structural frames. Provides rigidity without excessive weight.

Selecting the most appropriate stock form from the outset saves significant machining time and reduces material waste. If a component is essentially a hollow cylinder (such as a handrail or a bicycle fork), starting from tube rather than solid rod eliminates the need to bore out the centre — a time-consuming and wasteful operation. Similarly, using angle section for shelf brackets means the required L-shaped profile already exists; cutting it from flat plate would waste roughly half the material. Designers should always ask which stock form most closely matches the final component geometry before choosing a process.

Forces, Stresses and Work Hardening

When metals are in service they experience various forces. Understanding these helps designers choose the right metal and design to minimise failure:

  • Tension — a stretching force pulling the material apart (e.g. a lifting cable). Requires high tensile strength.
  • Compression — a squashing force (e.g. a column supporting a load). Cast iron performs well in compression.
  • Shear — forces acting in opposite directions across a cross-section (e.g. the force on a rivet holding two plates together).
  • Torsion — a twisting force (e.g. a drive shaft transmitting rotary motion from an engine to the wheels).

Work hardening occurs when a metal is repeatedly deformed at room temperature. Each deformation increases the dislocation density in the metal’s crystal structure, making it harder but less ductile. A paperclip repeatedly bent back and forth becomes harder and eventually snaps — this is work hardening in action. It can be useful (cold-drawing wire to increase its strength) or problematic (a sheet of metal becoming too brittle to bend further during forming).

The mechanical properties of steel are not fixed; they can be deliberately altered by carefully controlled heating and cooling. This is because the crystal structure of iron changes at specific temperatures. By controlling the temperature and the rate of cooling, engineers can produce steels ranging from very soft and ductile (for forming) to extremely hard (for cutting tools). Heat treatment therefore gives designers a second layer of material selection: not just which steel to use, but which state to use it in.

Heat treatment processes are most commonly applied to carbon steels and high-speed steels. They are generally not used for mild steel (too little carbon to respond significantly) and cannot make non-ferrous metals such as aluminium hard in the same way, though aluminium alloys can be heat-treated to improve strength by a different mechanism (precipitation hardening).

Heat Treatment Processes

The main heat treatment processes for steel are annealing, hardening, tempering, normalising and case hardening. Each involves different temperatures and cooling rates, producing different outcomes:

  • Annealing — the steel is heated to a specific temperature (typically 700–900 °C depending on carbon content), held there to allow the crystal structure to reorganise, then cooled very slowly (usually by leaving it in the furnace to cool). The result is a soft, ductile metal that is easy to machine or form. Annealing is used to relieve internal stresses after welding or to restore ductility to work-hardened metal.
  • Hardening — the steel is heated above its critical temperature (typically 760–900 °C) until it glows orange/yellow, then quenched (plunged rapidly into water, oil or brine). The rapid cooling prevents the carbon atoms from migrating, locking a hard but brittle crystal structure (martensite) in place. The steel is now very hard but too brittle for most uses and must be tempered.
  • Tempering — always follows hardening. The hardened steel is reheated to a lower temperature (150–400 °C, depending on the required toughness), held briefly, then allowed to cool in air. This reduces some of the brittleness introduced by hardening while retaining most of the hardness. The temperature is judged by oxide colours that appear on polished steel: pale yellow (∼220 °C) for scrapers, blue (∼300 °C) for springs. Tempering produces a balance of hardness and toughness.
  • Normalising — similar to annealing but the steel is cooled in still air rather than in the furnace. This produces a slightly harder and stronger result than full annealing. Normalising is used to refine the grain structure after forging or hot rolling, producing a more uniform microstructure across the material.
  • Case hardening — used specifically for mild steel, which has too little carbon to be hardened by quenching alone. The surface is enriched with carbon (by heating in a carbon-rich medium such as charcoal powder) and then quenched. The result is a hard outer case with a tough, ductile core. This combination is ideal for gear teeth and camshafts, which need a wear-resistant surface but a core that can absorb impact without shattering.
Key Fact

Hardening makes steel very hard but brittle; it is always followed by tempering to restore some toughness. Annealing (furnace cool) produces the softest result; normalising (air cool) gives a slightly stronger outcome. Case hardening applies only to mild steel and produces a hard surface over a tough core.
exam_tip_html: Questions on heat treatment commonly ask you to “describe” a named process: always state the material it applies to, the temperature range, the cooling method and the resulting property change. A complete answer for hardening would be: “High carbon steel is heated to approximately 760–900 °C until it glows orange, then quenched rapidly in water or oil. This locks the hard martensite structure, making the steel very hard but brittle.” Omitting the cooling method or the property outcome will lose marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Metal selection is driven by function, cost, aesthetics, availability and environment; no single factor is sufficient, and a complete exam answer must address at least two.
  • Metals are supplied in stock forms (sheet, plate, bar, rod, tube, angle); choosing the right form reduces waste and simplifies manufacture.
  • Heat treatment processes alter the properties of steel: annealing softens; hardening (followed by tempering) increases hardness and toughness; normalising refines grain structure; case hardening gives mild steel a hard surface with a tough core.

glossary_terms.definition: The standard shapes and sizes in which raw materials are supplied by manufacturers, such as sheet, plate, bar, rod, tube and angle section.
The increase in hardness and decrease in ductility that occurs when a metal is repeatedly bent or cold-worked, caused by the build-up of dislocations in its crystal structure.
Rapid cooling of heated metal by plunging it into a liquid such as water, oil or brine; used in hardening to lock a hard but brittle crystal structure in place.
A heat treatment process that enriches the surface of mild steel with carbon before quenching, producing a hard outer case with a tough, ductile core.

practice_questions.text:
Which heat treatment process produces the softest, most ductile result in steel?
A) Hardening
B) Tempering
C) Annealing
D) Case hardening
Name two stock forms in which aluminium sheet metal is commercially supplied.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: sheet / plate / bar / rod / tube / angle section. Must be standard stock forms. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to mild steel during work hardening.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• When mild steel is repeatedly bent or cold-worked, dislocations build up in its crystal structure.
• This makes the metal progressively harder.
• However, the metal also becomes less ductile (more brittle) and will eventually crack or fracture if deformation continues. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the hardening process must always be followed by tempering.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hardening (heating then rapid quenching) produces a very hard but extremely brittle crystal structure in the steel.
• A hardened but untempered steel would fracture under impact or shock loading, making it unsuitable for most applications.
• Tempering reheats the hardened steel to a lower temperature (150-400°C), which relieves internal stresses and allows some ductility to return.
• The result is a steel that retains much of its hardness while gaining enough toughness to withstand the forces in service, e.g. a chisel blade that cuts without shattering.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why case hardening is used for the gear teeth of a bicycle gearbox rather than simply using high carbon steel throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gear teeth need a very hard, wear-resistant surface to withstand repeated metal-to-metal contact without deteriorating.
• The core of the gear must be tough enough to absorb the shock loads transmitted by rapid gear changes without fracturing.
• High carbon steel throughout would be hard but brittle: the entire gear, including the root of each tooth, would be at risk of sudden fracture under impact.
• Case hardening on mild steel addresses both requirements: the surface is enriched with carbon and quenched to produce a hard case, while the mild steel core remains tough and ductile.
• This combination extends product life and improves safety compared to a uniformly hard but brittle gear.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both surface and core requirements explained, mechanism of case hardening described, compared to alternative with reference to product context. Secure: Both requirements and the process described but comparison limited. Developing: Process described but link to product requirements thin. Emerging: Superficial reference to hardening without explaining the case/core distinction.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using titanium rather than mild steel for the frame of a high-performance bicycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of titanium:
• Titanium has an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio; a titanium frame can be as strong as steel at a fraction of the mass, reducing overall bicycle weight and improving performance.
• Titanium is highly corrosion resistant without any surface treatment, making it suitable for use in wet, muddy and salty conditions without rusting.
• Titanium has a degree of flex that can provide a more comfortable ride than the stiffer steel alternative.
• Long service life means less frequent replacement; over a lifetime the higher initial cost may be offset.
Disadvantages of titanium:
• Titanium costs approximately 50 times more per kilogram than mild steel, making titanium frames prohibitively expensive for most consumers.
• Titanium is significantly more difficult to machine and weld; it must be welded in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, requiring specialist equipment and skilled labour, further increasing cost.
• Titanium is less readily available than mild steel, making repairs in the field or by a local welder less practical.
• Mild steel frames can be easily repaired, reshaped and sourced cheaply; this is a significant advantage for budget and touring cyclists.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, linked to bicycle performance and manufacturing context. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; limited balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

flashcard_questions.q: Name five factors a designer considers when selecting a metal.
flashcard_questions.a: Selection depends on the part's function and cost, as well as its appearance, how available the metal is, and environmental impact.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between metal sheet and plate?
flashcard_questions.a: Sheet is under 3 mm thick; plate is 3 mm or more.
Repeated cold-working builds up dislocations, increasing hardness and reducing ductility.
Steel is heated then cooled very slowly in the furnace, producing a soft, ductile structure.
Rapidly cooling heated metal in water, oil or brine to lock in a hard crystal structure.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must hardening always be followed by tempering?
flashcard_questions.a: Hardening makes steel very hard but brittle; tempering restores some toughness.

flashcard_questions.q: What temperature range is used for tempering steel?
flashcard_questions.a: Typically 150 to 400 degrees Celsius, depending on the toughness required.

flashcard_questions.q: What does normalising do to steel and how does it differ from annealing?
flashcard_questions.a: Both refine grain structure, but normalising cools in still air, giving a slightly harder result.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of steel is used for case hardening and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Mild steel; it has too little carbon to harden fully, so the surface is enriched with carbon first.

flashcard_questions.q: What combination of properties does case hardening produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A hard, wear-resistant outer case with a tough, ductile core.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one application where case hardening is the appropriate treatment.
flashcard_questions.a: Gear teeth or camshafts, which need a hard surface but a core that absorbs impact.

flashcard_questions.q: What force acts on a rivet holding two plates together?
flashcard_questions.a: Shear force, acting in opposite directions across the rivet's cross-section.
